title: Health, antibiotics and the humanitarian squeeze in wartime Ukraine
label: 3 November 2026 · Humanitarian situation in Ukraine
summary: Experts and Ukrainian humanitarian leaders told MPs that Ukraine’s healthcare reforms, carried out during a major war, have left hospitals understaffed and underfunded just as multi‑drug resistant infections and damage to medical supply chains are rising. Witnesses warned reserve antibiotics are scarce, diagnostics and infection control are weak, and power and logistics attacks are disrupting medicines and aid. They urged tailored international support: finance for essential drugs, national treatment guidance, better logistics, and stronger partnerships with local NGOs.

chapters.title: Hospitals under strain: reforms, staff and infection control
chapters.takeaway: Ukraine’s healthcare reform, started during full-scale war, has left hospitals consolidated, underfunded and short of staff, making infection control and treatment of resistant infections much harder.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We’re looking at the humanitarian situation in Ukraine—let’s start with the health system. Elena, can you give an overview?

turns.speaker: Dr Elena Moshynets
turns.text: Ukraine began a big healthcare reform in 2022 to align with Western systems, but it launched during the invasion and wasn’t adapted for wartime. Hospitals are being merged and asked to do more without extra money, staff or equipment.

turns.speaker: Dr Elena Moshynets
turns.text: Infection prevention is collapsing: nurses cover 40–60 beds in some places, staffing and pay are low, and that makes basic infection control very difficult to maintain.

turns.speaker: Tracy Gilbert
turns.text: Dr Moore, can you explain why antimicrobial resistance matters beyond a single infection?

turns.speaker: Dr Luke Moore
turns.text: If antibiotics stop working, routine surgery, chemotherapy, implants and diabetic care all become much riskier. Bacteria reproduce and adapt quickly, while new antibiotics take years and lots of money to develop.

turns.speaker: Dr Luke Moore
turns.text: Conflict makes things worse: wounded people with resistant infections can spread those bacteria in crowded hospitals, and displaced patients carry resistant bugs across borders.

turns.speaker: David Mundell
turns.text: How are you collaborating internationally to tackle conflict wound infections?

turns.speaker: Dr Luke Moore
turns.text: We’ve built a network with Ukrainian researchers, UK hospitals and universities. UK Defence Innovation (part of the MOD) funded a formal project to map which bugs exist, what drugs still work, and to deploy diagnostics closer to the frontline.

turns.speaker: Dr Elena Moshynets
turns.text: There aren’t enough infection‑control specialists in Ukraine to meet the reform’s new requirements. The reform expects hospitals to implement complex systems that they simply cannot staff or pay for right now.

chapters.title: Antibiotics, diagnostics and a dangerous funding gap
chapters.takeaway: Many hospitals lack 'reserve' antibiotics, diagnostics are underused because treatment can’t be guaranteed, and national guidance needs to be realistic and funded.

turns.speaker: Tulip Siddiq
turns.text: How available are antibiotics in Ukraine, and how does that affect resistance?

turns.speaker: Dr Elena Moshynets
turns.text: Many reserve antibiotics aren’t registered or are too expensive for hospitals. Clinicians sometimes must prescribe what’s in stock or tell patients to buy drugs themselves—undermining stewardship and ethics.

turns.speaker: Dr Luke Moore
turns.text: There are also counterfeit or degraded medicines because supply chains and cold storage get damaged in conflict. Diagnostics can be cheaper in the long run, but when drug budgets are tight people guess instead of testing.

turns.speaker: Noah Law
turns.text: Were these reforms needed? What went wrong with their timing?

turns.speaker: Dr Elena Moshynets
turns.text: Reforms aimed to reach Western standards, which is positive, but they should have been gradual—15–20 years is realistic. Rolling them out fast in wartime without resources, workforce or adaptation has created gaps.

turns.speaker: Dr Elena Moshynets
turns.text: Ukraine needs nationally co‑ordinated, evidence‑based guidelines that reflect local resistance patterns and what drugs are realistically available and funded.

turns.speaker: Dr Luke Moore
turns.text: The WHO asked countries for national AMR plans; many exist but are copy‑pasted. WHO should help countries learn from each other about practical, low‑cost measures and support diagnostics and tech that work in conflict and remote settings.

chapters.title: Civilian harm, energy attacks and supply chains
chapters.takeaway: Long‑range strikes and drones are increasingly hitting cities, energy and storage, cutting off services, damaging medical warehouses and making winter preparedness critical.

turns.speaker: Alina Belobra
turns.text: This year the protection crisis worsened: longer‑range missiles and drones hit big cities and infrastructure. In July the monthly child death toll was the highest in four years.

turns.speaker: Alina Belobra
turns.text: Attacks on energy, telecoms, rail and warehouses cut people off from services and disrupt medical supply chains. Keeping cold‑chain medicine near the front is especially hard.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You used the phrase 'human safaris'—what does that mean?

turns.speaker: Alina Belobra
turns.text: It’s a local term for targeted drone attacks that pick civilians or vehicles as targets, ignoring the rules that should protect civilians; this makes markets and hospitals unsafe in places like Kherson.

turns.speaker: David Mundell
turns.text: Are humanitarian warehouses being hit?

turns.speaker: Illya Kletskovskyy
turns.text: Yes—several warehouses have been damaged, including two large Red Cross warehouses. The pattern looks like economic warfare: attacks deliberately hit logistics, businesses and stores to pressure the population.

turns.speaker: Alina Belobra
turns.text: NGOs report it’s harder to store and transport medicines near the front. Some groups are dispersing stocks and using small, underground or local storage, but winter and blackouts make this precarious.

chapters.title: Local NGOs, volunteers and the logistics squeeze
chapters.takeaway: Local civil society are the first responders and need more predictable funding, inclusion in World Bank/State programmes, local procurement, and support for volunteer wellbeing.

turns.speaker: Mila Leonova
turns.text: Local NGOs and volunteer groups were the first responders in 2022 and have professionalised. They now run big programmes—evacuations, shelter, livelihoods—and must be part of planning with Government and donors.

turns.speaker: Alex Sobel
turns.text: How have UK loan guarantees and World Bank funds helped?

turns.speaker: Mila Leonova
turns.text: Those funds are valuable, but the World Bank mainly channels money through Government and firms. Civil society needs clearer routes to access those funds and to form pooled financing with private partners.

turns.speaker: David Taylor
turns.text: Are border delays affecting supplies?

turns.speaker: Illya Kletskovskyy
turns.text: Yes. With ports and roads damaged, overland corridors—especially via Poland—are congested. Customs and longer queues slow humanitarian deliveries. Procuring more in Ukraine helps, but some items still must come from abroad.

turns.speaker: David Taylor
turns.text: What about logistics firms like Nova Poshta?

turns.speaker: Illya Kletskovskyy
turns.text: Nova Poshta has partnered with humanitarian groups and used to provide more pro bono support. They still help but have been affected by attacks themselves, so capacity varies.

turns.speaker: Brian Mathew
turns.text: How are volunteers holding up after years of conflict?

turns.speaker: Illya Kletskovskyy
turns.text: Volunteer numbers surged early in the war but many are fatigued. Long spells of frontline response and winter needs create mental health and retention issues; volunteers need structured support and respite.

turns.speaker: Alina Belobra
turns.text: We also see people self‑evacuating or returning home and falling through formal aid systems. Localised, flexible aid and support for social services in receiving communities are vital.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If you had three practical asks of the international community, what would they be?

turns.speaker: Dr Elena Moshynets
turns.text: Fund and guarantee national access to reserve antibiotics and diagnostics, and help create national treatment guidelines adapted to Ukraine’s resistance patterns and budgets.

turns.speaker: Dr Luke Moore
turns.text: WHO should curate and share practical, low‑cost AMR measures across countries, and fund deployable diagnostics and data tools so remote or conflict areas can identify and manage infections fast.

turns.speaker: Mila Leonova
turns.text: Include Ukrainian civil society in World Bank and donor planning, fund localisation, and build public‑private‑civil society partnerships to support livelihoods and recovery as well as immediate aid.

turns.speaker: Illya Kletskovskyy
turns.text: Support the humanitarian–development nexus so emergency aid links to recovery programmes, and back systems that keep supplies moving despite attacks and border congestion.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. This has painted a stark but practical picture: health systems and antibiotics are brittle, supply chains and civilians are under direct attack, and local NGOs are stretched but essential. We will take these recommendations forward.
